# Mahāgovinda Sutta (DN 19 (PTS DN ii 220))

**ID:** DN 19 (PTS DN ii 220)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāgovinda Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Great Steward
**PTS:** DN ii 220
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn19
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāgovinda Sutta* is the nineteenth discourse of the *Dīgha Nikāya* and the sixth sutta in its *Mahāvagga* [Nguyen Van Thuong; SuttaCentral]. Framed as a narrative delivered to the Buddha by the gandhabba Pañcasikha regarding the assemblies of the gods, it recounts how Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra praised the ancient high steward (Mahāgovinda), whom the Buddha reveals to have been a previous incarnation of himself [Nguyen Van Thuong; SuttaCentral]. Recognized as an early canonical "Suttanta Jātaka" embedded within the sutta collections, the story relates how the bodhisatta served as a royal courtier to King Reṇu in Jambudvīpa, later renounced worldly life along with many followers, practiced the boundless states (such as intense cultivation of compassion during a rains retreat to commune with Brahmā), and guided disciples to rebirth in the Brahma realms [Appleton 2012; Dhammapala et al. 1984; Gaffney 2003; Nguyen Van Thuong]. The Buddha concludes by contrasting this fruitful path to divine rebirth with his own teaching leading directly to nibbāna [Appleton 2012; Nguyen Van Thuong].

The sutta is widely witnessed across early Buddhist traditions. Beyond the Pāli Theravāda version, ancient versions survive in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit within the Lokottaravādin *Mahāvastu* and in Sanskrit manuscript fragments from Central Asia (Turfan), which Dieter Schlingloff discussed [Dhammapala et al. 1984; Lamotte 1988; Nakamura 1980; Tournier et al. 2018]. In Chinese translation, it is preserved in the *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 3, *Dian zun jing* 典尊經) and as an independent translation (*Dajianku polomen yuanqi jing* 大堅固婆羅門緣起經, T 8) [Cheng 2014; Dhammapala et al. 1984; Tournier et al. 2018; SuttaCentral]. Both SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus align these Dīrghāgama versions and the *Mahāvastu* recension with the Pāli text, noting also Tibetan parallels in the *Vinayavastu* and *Karmaśataka* [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. In Sanskrit and Chinese collections, the sutta was frequently grouped in the same section (*varga*) as the *Janavasabha Sutta* (DN 18), a relationship reflected in DharmaNexus data showing that DN 19 shares its largest internal reuse block with DN 18 (over 20,000 matching characters) [DharmaNexus; Tournier et al. 2018].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for dn19 — Basic metadata, English title, blurb, and curated parallel records.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel match data for PA_dn_19 — Text reuse calculations showing extensive shared passages with DN 18 and alignment scores with the Mahāvastu, DĀ 3, and T 8.
- [Appleton 2012] Naomi Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-life Stories — Identifies the sutta as an early embedded jātaka contrasting rebirth in heavenly realms with the Buddha's path to nibbāna.
- [Dhammapala et al. 1984] Gatare Dhammapala, Richard Gombrich, K. R. Norman (eds.), Buddhist Studies in Honour of Hammalava Saddhatissa (1984) — Discusses the four sectarian versions (Pāli, Sanskrit Mahāvastu, and two Chinese translations) and the setting in Reṇu's kingdom.
- [Lamotte 1988] Étienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988) — Notes the citation of the Mahāgovindasutta in the Mahāvastu.
- [Nakamura 1980] Hajime Nakamura, Indian Buddhism: A Survey with Bibliographical Notes (1980) — Records Dieter Schlingloff's study of Sanskrit fragments of the sutta.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, Jātakanidānakathā: A critical study (2003) — Notes the practice of the brahmavihāras in the sutta.
- [Nguyen Van Thuong] Bhikkhu T.M.T. Nguyen Van Thuong, Study of the Concept of Citta as Depicted in the Pali Tipitaka — Provides details on setting, Pañcasikha, Sanankumāra, Karuṇā meditation, and the Suttanta Jātaka genre.
- [Tournier et al. 2018] Vincent Tournier, Vincent Eltschinger, Marta Sernesi (eds.), Archaeologies of the Written (2018) — Discusses the association of Mahāgovinda with Janavasabha in the Chinese and Central Asian Dīrghāgamas.
- [Cheng 2014] Fung Kei Cheng, Conceptualising a Bodhisattva-Spirit-Oriented Counselling Framework (2014) — Attests the Chinese parallel title T 8 (Dajianku polomen yuanqi jing).
